analysis.one_liner: Sets uniform patient-protection rules for employer and private health plans, including appeals, emergency care, and direct specialist access.
analysis.headline: A Georgia Republican introduced the bill with one Democratic cosponsor, it was sent to three House committees, and it never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written a set of patient protections into federal law for everyone with job-based or private health coverage. Plans would have had to run medical reviews under written clinical rules, give patients internal and external appeals when claims are denied, pay emergency-room claims without prior approval, let women see an OB-GYN without a referral, let children see a pediatrician directly, cover routine costs of approved clinical trials, cover medically needed non-formulary drugs, and pay claims promptly. It also would have barred plans from stopping doctors from telling patients about their treatment options, and removed a legal shield that kept patients from suing many employer plans.
analysis.who_benefits: People enrolled in employer group health plans and private insurance, especially those denied coverage for a treatment, needing emergency care, seeing specialists for serious ongoing conditions, or seeking care outside their plan's network. Doctors also gain protection against plan gag rules and denials.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with employer or private insurance

how_it_helps.text: Every covered plan must run an appeals process: internal review by a professional who did not make the initial denial, with 14-day deadlines (72 hours in urgent cases), and an external appeal decided by an independent panel of at least three clinical peers that is binding on the plan [S2][S3].

Plans could not require prior authorization for emergency services, and patients could not be billed more than in-network cost sharing when they use an emergency department, under a 'prudent layperson' standard [S2][S3].
Plans could not require a referral or authorization for obstetrical or gynecological care, and children could be assigned a pediatrician as their primary care provider [S2][S3].

Plans must provide exceptions to drug formulary limits when a non-formulary drug is medically indicated, and must cover routine patient costs for people in approved clinical trials for life-threatening illnesses [S2][S3].

The bill bans financial incentives that encourage denials of claims in utilization review, requires plans to pay claims promptly, and voids any contract provision that stops a doctor from advising a patient about their health status or treatment options [S3].

It amends ERISA, the law that had prevented many patients with employer coverage from suing their plan over denied care, to remove that preemption for certain actions involving health insurance policyholders [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers that sponsor group health plans would bear the cost of compliance: outside reviewers for external appeals, written review programs, timely claim payment, and the coverage itself when appeals reverse denials. Insurers could pass some costs into premiums, and enrollees choosing the required point-of-service option pay its extra premium and cost sharing themselves.

drawbacks.text: The added requirements — independent external review panels, strict deadlines, prompt payment, and more coverage when denials are overturned — are real costs for insurers and self-insured employers, and some of that cost would surface in premiums for everyone [S3].

The required out-of-network (consumer choice) option lets the issuer charge extra premiums and cost sharing for it, with the bill stating the extra amounts 'shall be borne by the enrollee' — so real choice of doctors can come at a price patients pay themselves [S3].

Critics of a federal patient-protection standard argued it overrides state regulation of insurance and adds federal bureaucracy on top of the state rules many states had already adopted; the bill itself wrestles with this, including a preemption and 'state flexibility' section [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are substantial for patients — binding external appeals, emergency coverage without prior approval, direct access to OB-GYNs and pediatricians, and the end of gag clauses — and they mirror rules that later became standard in health law. The main honest objection is cost: insurers and employers would pay for outside reviewers and more overturned denials, and some would show up in premiums, with the out-of-network option's extra cost falling on the enrollees who choose it. On balance the bill targeted a documented problem — plans denying care and restricting doctors — with rules that largely match what eventually became federal practice.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees, each of which passed it down to a health subcommittee, and no committee ever reported it or brought it to the floor before the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Rep. Charlie Norwood (R-GA) introduced the bill on February 12, 2007, joined by Rep. John Dingell (D-MI) as its cosponsor [S1][S3][S4].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, and Ways and Means Committees on the day of introduction [S1][S5].

In the following months the committees referred it to their health subcommittees — the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health on February 13, 2007, again on March 7, and the Education and Labor Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions on June 5 [S5].
No committee ever reported the bill, no subcommittee or full-chamber action followed, and the bill died when the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed care plans were better off: the bill died without a vote, so they never faced the binding external appeals process, emergency-coverage mandates, prompt-payment rules, or penalties for refusing externally approved care that the bill would have imposed. Patients with employer coverage remained under the existing, more limited rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and managed care plans

for.name: Rep. Charlie Norwood
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, reviving his earlier bipartisan 'patients' bill of rights' framework

for.name: Rep. John Dingell
for.role: U.S. Representative, Michigan; bill cosponsor and ranking member (later chair) of the Energy and Commerce Committee

against.name: House committee leadership (Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, Ways and Means)
against.role: Chairs of the committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to health subcommittees and never reported it to the full House, leaving it without a path to a vote

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by a Republican and cosponsored by a senior Democrat, but it never reached a floor vote, so no roll calls show how the parties would have split.

industries.industry: Health insurers and managed care plans
industries.note: The bill forces them to cover emergency care without prior approval, submit denials to binding independent review, pay claims promptly, and accept penalties up to $1,000 a day for refusing externally approved benefits. Their revenue partly depends on denying or delaying claims, so these rules run directly against their bottom line.

industries.industry: Self-insured employers sponsoring group health plans
industries.note: The bill applies its patient-protection standards to group health plans under ERISA and the tax code, adding compliance costs for employers that run their own plans. Employers' interest in keeping plan costs down is in tension with the patient protections.

industries.industry: Independent external appeal and utilization review entities
industries.note: Every plan must contract with certified independent external appeal entities and run structured utilization review programs, creating a new paid market for medical review firms. Their interest runs alongside patients', since they are paid to review denials independently.
